overview: This file concerns the November 1940 replacement of Admiral Seizō Kobayashi by Admiral Kiyoshi Hasegawa as Governor-General of Japanese-ruled Taiwan (Formosa). Diplomatic and naval reporting from Tokyo interpreted Hasegawa’s retention on the active naval list as evidence that the governorship was intended to coordinate Japan’s southward expansion rather than merely administer the colony, possibly anticipating the integration of Taiwan with the Japanese South Seas Mandate. An internal memorandum also reviews the roles of Hasegawa, Koshirō Oikawa, Kōichi Shiozawa, and Kichisaburō Nomura in Japanese naval operations at Shanghai in 1932 and 1937–38.

subfiles.title: Memorandum to Hornbeck on Japanese naval commanders at Shanghai
subfiles.about: The memorandum answers a question about which Japanese admirals commanded or directed naval landing forces at Shanghai in 1932 and later commanded there in 1937–38.
subfiles.summary: The writer states that Kiyoshi Hasegawa was Japanese naval commander in chief at Shanghai in 1937 and remained there until Koshirō Oikawa relieved him in April 1938. For the 1932 fighting, the memorandum identifies Kōichi Shiozawa, then chief of staff of the First Japanese Fleet, as particularly involved with the naval landings. Shiozawa was recalled and Kichisaburō Nomura was sent to Shanghai to take charge of the situation.

subfiles.title: Fragmentary inquiry concerning a commander in 1932
subfiles.about: A brief internal question, preserved in severely garbled OCR, appears to concern the identity or position of a chief or commander associated with events in 1932.
subfiles.summary: The page bears Department of State and Department of Political Relations headings. Its single substantive line is too badly corrupted to reconstruct confidently, but its reference to a “Chief” and 1932 likely records the inquiry answered by the memorandum on the preceding page.

subfiles.title: Telegram from Grew on Hasegawa’s appointment as Governor-General of Formosa
subfiles.about: Grew reports Hasegawa’s appointment as Governor-General of Formosa and the belief that it signaled greater emphasis on Japan’s southward advance.
subfiles.summary: The Tokyo press announced that Admiral Kobayashi had resigned and that Admiral Kiyoshi Hasegawa, a member of the Supreme War Council, would succeed him as Governor-General of Formosa. Hasegawa was reportedly to remain on active duty, which observers interpreted as evidence that the governorship had an operational role in organizing Japan’s advance to the south. The naval attaché asked that the Navy Department be informed, and the telegram was transmitted through Shanghai.

subfiles.title: Naval attaché report on the strategic meaning of Hasegawa’s appointment
subfiles.to: Office of the Chief of Naval Operations; information to the Assistant U.S. Naval Attaché, Shanghai, and Commander in Chief, Asiatic Fleet
subfiles.about: The naval attaché argues that Hasegawa’s appointment was intended to coordinate naval expansion into the South Seas rather than to provide routine colonial administration.
subfiles.summary: The report regards Hasegawa’s appointment and continued active-duty status as marking increased naval influence within the Japanese government. Because he had naval administrative experience but no colonial administrative experience, it concludes that his selection related to Japan’s southward strategy. It anticipates closer coordination between Taiwan and the South Seas administration, possibly including the combination of the mandate islands with Taiwan, and compares the navy’s expected position there to the army’s entrenched position in Manchuria under General Umezu.

interest: The file is valuable because it shows American officials reading a colonial appointment as an indicator of Japanese strategic intentions rather than as a routine personnel change. The naval attaché’s prediction that Taiwan and the South Seas Mandate might be administratively combined provides unusually explicit contemporary evidence of how U.S. observers connected colonial government, naval influence, and southward expansion. The accompanying inquiry and memorandum also reveal the State Department’s effort to reconstruct Hasegawa’s earlier Shanghai record when assessing his new appointment.
